title: Tú or usted?
body: Spanish has two words for "you". Use tú with friends and family. Use usted with strangers and older people to be polite. The verb changes too: ¿Hablas inglés? (tú), ¿Habla inglés? (usted).

title: Saying where you are from
body: Use soy (I am) + de + a place: Soy de México. Use soy for your job too, with no "a": Soy estudiante. You can leave out yo (I), because soy already means "I am".

title: Every noun is el or la
body: Every Spanish noun is male (el) or female (la), even food. Most nouns ending in -o take el: el vino. Most ending in -a take la: la manzana. Learn each noun together with its el or la.

title: Two verbs for "to be"
body: Spanish has two verbs for "to be". Ser is for what someone is like: Él es alto. Estar is for how someone feels now: Estamos cansados. For a woman, -o often becomes -a: alta, cansada.

title: Verbs for "I" end in -o
body: Spanish verbs change their ending for each person. For "I", most verbs end in -o: hablar → hablo, comer → como, trabajar → trabajo. The ending already means "I", so yo is often left out.

title: Me gusta and me duele
body: To say you like something, Spanish says "it pleases me": Me gusta el café. Put no first to say you don't: No me gusta el té. Pain works the same way: Me duele la cabeza.

title: Describing words go after
body: Words that describe a noun usually come after it: un coche caro = an expensive car. They also change to match the noun: un día bonito, una ciudad bonita.
